title: Case study draft review (Northwind) - internal
topics: Narrative arc and headline: performance economics + Dedicated reliability
Proof/claims checklist and what we can publish (exact metrics vs ranges)
CTA placement and case study page layout
Distribution plan: blog, docs landing page, PDF 1-pager, outbound sequences, decks
Approval gating: Legal + customer review window + technical validation
next_steps: Ethan to revise draft for tighter problem/constraint framing and reduce jargon (due 2025-10-18)
Markus + Simran to confirm architecture diagram annotations and routing/fallback terminology (due 2025-10-18)
Tyler to propose UTM plan + distribution checklist for blog/newsletter/sales sequences (due 2025-10-21)
Michael to confirm standard metrics disclaimer + quote attribution language for Northwind (due 2025-10-21)
Camila + Soojin to align on publish date target and backup plan if customer legal review slips (due 2025-10-22)
summary: Internal review of the Northwind case study draft before customer review. Team agreed the story should lead with the business problem + constraints (p95 latency, cost ceilings, reliability), then show how Redwood Dedicated + routing/fallback + caching delivered outcomes. Marketing flagged a claims/proof checklist: any quantitative statement needs a source, timeframe, and disclaimers; prefer ranges if customer hesitates. CTA should appear once mid-page and once at the end, and the PDF 1-pager should map to the same narrative with a "Dedicated / Private" enterprise CTA. Distribution plan includes: docs Case Studies landing, blog post, sales deck insert slide, outbound sequence snippet, and a short enablement talk track. Risks: publishing exact metrics while a recent p95 spike is under investigation; ensure we do not imply "zero downtime" or make unqualified comparisons to named competitors.
questions: Do we publish exact numbers or ranges for p95 latency and $/1M tokens given customer sensitivity and recent variance?
Where should the architecture diagram live (in docs page only vs included in PDF), and how detailed can it be without exposing vendor specifics?
What is the minimum proof required for reliability claims (SLA language vs observed uptime)?
Can we mention "automatic fallback" without over-promising cross-region failover?
transcript:
Meeting: Case study draft review (Northwind) - internal
Date: 2025-10-16
Time: 10:02 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees (Redwood): Camila Reyes (VP Marketing), Soojin Lee (Product Marketing), Ethan Wallace (Writer/Editor), Markus Klein (Solutions Eng), Simran Kaur (Technical validation), Tyler Benson (Marketing Ops), Michael Grant (Legal)

---

[10:02:14] Camila Reyes: Alright, cool, I think we’ve got most folks. This is the internal pass on the Northwind customer story. Goal today is narrative, claims/proof checklist, CTA placement, and then how we’re gonna distribute this so Sales actually uses it.

[10:02:32] Soojin Lee: Yep. And I want to make sure we’re aligned with the messaging pillars we agreed on, like performance economics, reliability and fallbacks, and the deployment flexibility angle without it turning into a product brochure.

[10:02:46] Ethan Wallace: I can pull up the draft. Quick caveat, it’s still got some bracketed placeholders for metrics until we confirm what’s publishable.

[10:02:53] Tyler Benson: Also there’s like, five different versions floating around in Drive. If we can decide “this is the canonical doc,” I’ll lock it.

[10:03:03] Camila Reyes: Great. Ethan, give us the top-level structure in 60 seconds.

[10:03:09] Ethan Wallace: Sure. It’s Problem, Constraints, Solution, Implementation, Results, then “Why Redwood” and a CTA. Problem is: ecommerce search + chat assistant with traffic spikes, they needed p95 under a target, they were seeing cost creep, and they had reliability issues with… I didn’t name the prior provider, it’s generic.

[10:03:33] Soojin Lee: I like that we didn’t name them. Don’t do a “we beat X.” We can say “previous approach” or “previous provider” and then focus on outcomes.

[10:03:42] Markus Klein: On the Implementation section, we mention “routing and fallbacks” but it’s a little hand-wavy. I can help make it accurate without turning it into a kernel blog post.

[10:03:51] Simran Kaur: Yeah, the diagram block right now says “multi-region failover,” and that’s not what we set up for them. It’s more like model variant fallback + capacity tier fallback, and region is an option but not what they’re using today.

[10:04:05] Ethan Wallace: Got it. I probably over-interpreted a note from the intro call.

[10:04:09] Camila Reyes: Cool, we’ll fix. Let’s go section by section. Soojin, narrative feedback first.

[10:04:16] Soojin Lee: Big thing: we should lead with their constraints in plain language. Like, “holiday peaks, strict p95, cost per token ceiling.” Right now we start with “Redwood Dedicated provides…” and it’s like, nope, tell me why I care about Northwind first.

[10:04:34] Ethan Wallace: Totally fair.

[10:04:36] Soojin Lee: Second: don’t bury the “Dedicated vs Hosted” decision. That’s the enterprise signal. But frame it as what Northwind needed—predictable throughput, data isolation, and control over scaling policy—versus “Dedicated is better.”

[10:04:52] Camila Reyes: And I want one strong quote early. Like a pull quote in the first third. We’ve got a good one from the intro thread but it needs tightening.

[10:05:02] Ethan Wallace: The one that’s like “we stopped playing whack-a-mole with latency”? That one?

[10:05:05] Camila Reyes: Yes, that’s the vibe.

[10:05:07] Michael Grant: Just make sure if it’s a quote, we have explicit approval for the exact words. Editing for clarity is fine but don’t change meaning. And we need attribution rules: name/title or “VP Engineering, Northwind” depending on their preference.

[10:05:23] Soojin Lee: Also the “Results” section—today it reads like a benchmark report. We want: what changed operationally. Like: fewer incidents, faster rollouts, less time spent tuning. Even if we can’t publish precise metrics, we can say “reduced variance” or “more predictable p95.”

[10:05:41] Markus Klein: On that point, we should be careful with “reliability.” If we say “improved uptime,” we need a source, time window, and whether it’s measured at Redwood edge or at their app. Otherwise Legal’s gonna get nervous.

[10:05:53] Michael Grant: Exactly. Avoid absolute language: “eliminated downtime,” “zero outages,” “guaranteed,” that stuff. If it’s tied to an SLA, say “SLA-backed” and reference the SLA category, not a number, unless customer okays it.

[10:06:08] Camila Reyes: Let’s talk proof checklist. Soojin, can you summarize what claims we’re making and what proof we need attached?

[10:06:16] Soojin Lee: Yep. Categories:
1) Performance: p95 latency, throughput under peak.
2) Cost: $ per 1M tokens, or “reduced spend.”
3) Reliability: failover/fallback and operational stability.
4) Deployment: Dedicated sizing, isolation.
5) Tooling: Console visibility, Optimize recs.

For any number, we need baseline vs after, timeframe, and measurement method. And ideally link back to the metrics worksheet internally, not public.

[10:06:48] Tyler Benson: Plus, for the web page, we need a standard metrics disclaimer block. Like “results will vary; metrics are customer-reported; measured over X.” We should reuse across stories so we’re consistent.

[10:07:02] Ethan Wallace: There’s an open question on whether we publish exact p95 and exact cost reduction or just ranges.

[10:07:09] Camila Reyes: Yeah, we need a decision guideline. Michael?

[10:07:12] Michael Grant: From a risk standpoint, ranges are easier. Exact numbers invite re-litigation later if a prospect reads it as a guarantee. But it’s also a marketing tradeoff—numbers sell.

[10:07:25] Markus Klein: Technically, I’d rather publish a range with a timeframe and condition, because performance is distribution-dependent. If we say “p95 180ms,” someone will ask “for what prompt length, what output length, what model?” and we’re not going to include that.

[10:07:41] Simran Kaur: Also, we had that support ticket this week about a transient p95 spike. It’s resolved, but if they’re reviewing the draft and we claim “stable p95,” they may push back.

[10:07:52] Camila Reyes: That’s the SUP-3812 thing, right? The latency spike during the interview window.

[10:07:56] Simran Kaur: Yeah. It was a brief period, and we mitigated, but optics matter.

[10:08:02] Soojin Lee: So let’s do: “reduced p95 latency by ~30–40%” or “cut p95 latency by a third,” something like that, if approved. Or “improved p95” without numbers if they won’t.

[10:08:16] Ethan Wallace: And on cost, same approach? Like “reduced per-token cost by 20–30%.”

[10:08:20] Michael Grant: If we do that, we must be explicit about the basis: “customer-reported,” “measured over X weeks,” and not “compared to all providers.”

[10:08:31] Tyler Benson: We can standardize the footnote. I’ll draft a disclaimer that’s consistent with our docs PR language.

[10:08:38] Camila Reyes: Great. Now CTA placement. The current draft has the CTA only at the bottom. I want one mid-page after Results, then again at the end.

[10:08:49] Soojin Lee: Agree. Also the CTA should be specific to the audience. For enterprise pipeline it’s “Talk to us about Dedicated or Private,” not “Sign up.” We can still link to docs but the primary is demo/contact.

[10:09:03] Tyler Benson: And for outbound sequences, we need a short “snippet” paragraph that AEs can paste. Like 3 bullets: use case, deployment type, outcomes, then a link.

[10:09:13] Camila Reyes: Yes. Also Sales asked for a one-slide deck insert. We should plan that now, not later.

[10:09:21] Ethan Wallace: I can distill the story into slide form. But we’ll need the final approved quote and whatever metrics are allowed.

[10:09:29] Markus Klein: Slide should include architecture diagram? Or too much?

[10:09:33] Soojin Lee: I’d keep the diagram on the web page, maybe a simplified block diagram in the PDF/slide. Otherwise it becomes “how to build it,” not “why it matters.”

[10:09:46] Simran Kaur: If we include any diagram, I want a review pass. People draw arrows that imply product features we don’t have.

[10:09:53] Camila Reyes: You’ll get a review pass, yes. Distribution plan. Tyler, talk through it.

[10:09:59] Tyler Benson: Plan:
- Publish on docs site under Case Studies landing. That’s the canonical URL.
- Blog post version: we can either re-post full text or do a shorter “story + link.” I’d recommend short blog so SEO doesn’t duplicate docs.
- PDF 1-pager for Sales: in the sales enablement folder, and link in HubSpot templates.
- Outbound: add a snippet to the enterprise sequences, plus a “late-stage objection handler” email.
- Deck insert: one slide “Northwind: Dedicated + fallbacks = predictable p95.”
- Internal enablement: 15-minute slot at Sales standup + CS sync.

[10:10:39] Camila Reyes: Good. Also newsletter and social? Or do we keep it quiet?

[10:10:44] Soojin Lee: Depends on customer comfort with logo visibility. If they’re okay with public logo, we can do a low-key LinkedIn post from company page. If they want limited, we keep it as “sales asset first.”

[10:10:58] Michael Grant: Exactly. Consent language usually specifies channels: website, blog, sales decks, events. If they exclude social, don’t do social.

[10:11:08] Ethan Wallace: For the blog short version, I’ll need guidance on tone. Developer-first, less marketing fluff, right?

[10:11:13] Camila Reyes: Yes. Avoid “revolutionary.” Keep it like, “Here’s what they built, here were constraints, here’s what changed.”

[10:11:23] Markus Klein: Also: define terms. If we say “KV cache,” we might lose people. But the audience is technical. We can say “caching and batching” without deep details.

[10:11:34] Soojin Lee: Right. “Smart batching and caching” is fine. Save KV cache talk for a DevEx blog.

[10:11:41] Camila Reyes: Let’s go deeper on the claims section, because I want a clear internal checklist before we send to Northwind. Ethan, read the “Results” bullets.

[10:11:50] Ethan Wallace: Okay, current bullets:
- “Reduced p95 latency by 38% under peak traffic.”
- “Lowered inference cost by 27% using batching and caching recommendations.”
- “Improved reliability with automatic fallback to compatible model variants.”
- “Faster rollouts with model version pinning and canary policies.”

[10:12:13] Soojin Lee: Love the structure.

[10:12:15] Michael Grant: Too specific for now. Those exact percentages need sign-off, and also: “automatic fallback” is okay if we define what fallback means. But “improved reliability” needs a qualifier.

[10:12:28] Markus Klein: On rollouts, we should confirm they actually used canary. They might have used a manual staged rollout. Don’t invent.

[10:12:36] Simran Kaur: Yes, I think they did a manual two-phase deploy. Not sure about A/B.

[10:12:41] Ethan Wallace: I’ll change “canary policies” to “staged rollouts” until confirmed.

[10:12:47] Camila Reyes: So, we’ll do ranges for the first two, confirm with Northwind. For reliability: maybe “added fallback paths to keep the app responsive during capacity constraints.” That’s more accurate.

[10:13:01] Soojin Lee: And add a line that’s operational: “reduced on-call escalations related to inference.” If we can’t quantify, it’s still meaningful.

[10:13:12] Michael Grant: That’s fine as long as it’s their statement, not ours. “According to Northwind, their team saw fewer after-hours escalations.”

[10:13:23] Tyler Benson: For the web layout, I want to propose a standardized “Metrics” module. Three cards with metric name, value (range), and footnote. Then a “How they built it” module with the diagram.

[10:13:37] Camila Reyes: That matches the design ticket. Okay.

[10:13:41] Markus Klein: On the diagram: it should show Redwood Dedicated cluster, their app, and where routing policy sits. But don’t show specific GPU types or counts unless approved.

[10:13:52] Simran Kaur: Right. If we say “H100s,” people will assume that’s required. Better to say “Dedicated GPU capacity” and keep it abstract.

[10:14:02] Soojin Lee: Also: we should mention Console. One sentence: “Console provided token-level latency and cost breakdowns that helped them tune.” That’s a differentiator.

[10:14:13] Ethan Wallace: I have a paragraph on Console but it’s maybe too long.

[10:14:17] Camila Reyes: Keep it short and concrete.

[10:14:20] Tyler Benson: Practical question: where do we host the PDF? Drive link dies sometimes. Should we put it in the sales enablement repository and link from there?

[10:14:29] Camila Reyes: Yes. And also attach in HubSpot templates.

[10:14:33] Tyler Benson: Okay, I’ll handle.

[10:14:36] Camila Reyes: What about outbound sequences—Soojin, can you propose the core talk track line?

[10:14:43] Soojin Lee: Something like: “Northwind moved an ecommerce assistant from a shared endpoint to Redwood Dedicated to meet peak p95 targets, cut unit costs with batching/caching, and keep responses stable via fallback routing.” Then link. Done.

[10:15:03] Markus Klein: Just don’t say “shared endpoint” if we can’t confirm their prior architecture. Maybe “from their prior approach.”

[10:15:10] Soojin Lee: Fair. “From their prior provider.”

[10:15:13] Michael Grant: Avoid “provider” if it suggests they had a contract breach or something. It’s fine, just be neutral.

[10:15:19] Camila Reyes: Let’s talk gating/approvals. Timeline: We want this live end of month-ish. Ethan, what’s your realistic revision turnaround?

[10:15:28] Ethan Wallace: I can get a revised draft by Saturday. Then we do one more internal proof pass Monday, then send to Northwind Tuesday.

[10:15:37] Camila Reyes: Works. Michael, what review window do we give them?

[10:15:41] Michael Grant: Standard is 10 business days, but we can ask for 5 business days if they’ve already seen the consent draft and they’re motivated. Just be prepared it slips.

[10:15:52] Tyler Benson: If it slips, our distribution schedule slips too. We can still prepare the sales slide internally, but no external use.

[10:16:01] Camila Reyes: Exactly. Okay, any other narrative issues?

[10:16:06] Soojin Lee: Small one: the “Why Redwood” section should not be a feature list. It should connect back to their constraints. Three bullets max.

[10:16:16] Ethan Wallace: Got it. I’ll rework to: “Predictable throughput,” “cost controls with visibility,” “graceful degradation / fallback.”

[10:16:25] Markus Klein: And define fallback precisely. Like, “fallback to pre-approved model variants when capacity is constrained.”

[10:16:33] Simran Kaur: Yes, and don’t promise “cross-region failover.”

[10:16:38] Camila Reyes: Cool. Quick check: do we mention Dedicated vs Private?

[10:16:44] Soojin Lee: In this story, it’s Dedicated. But the end CTA can say “Dedicated or Private” for prospects who need VPC. We should avoid implying Northwind is Private.

[10:16:55] Michael Grant: And don’t mention their security posture if not relevant. No “SOC2” claims tied to them.

[10:17:03] Ethan Wallace: Understood.

[10:17:05] Camila Reyes: Let’s do a fast pass on “things to remove” list.

[10:17:10] Soojin Lee: Remove: “best-in-class,” “industry-leading,” anything like that.

[10:17:15] Markus Klein: Remove: specific GPU SKUs and kernel references.

[10:17:19] Simran Kaur: Remove: “multi-region” and “automatic failover” unless confirmed.

[10:17:24] Michael Grant: Remove: “guarantee,” “ensured,” “eliminated.”

[10:17:29] Tyler Benson: Remove: multiple CTAs. Keep it clean.

[10:17:32] Camila Reyes: Great. What to add?

[10:17:35] Soojin Lee: Add: one sentence about evaluation/quality monitoring if they did it. Even “prompt set regression checks.” That’s a strong “production” signal.

[10:17:46] Markus Klein: They did run a small eval harness. Not huge, but yes. We can say “validated outputs with a prompt set before rollout.”

[10:17:55] Ethan Wallace: Perfect. I’ll incorporate.

[10:17:58] Camila Reyes: Alright, last topic: distribution ownership. Tyler owns operational distribution, Soojin owns talk track and messaging, Ethan owns copy, Markus and Simran own technical accuracy, Michael owns legal language. I’ll quarterback and handle exec visibility.

[10:18:15] Tyler Benson: Works.

[10:18:16] Camila Reyes: Any other risks we’re missing?

[10:18:20] Michael Grant: Just one. If we publish ranges, be consistent across assets. Don’t put “30–40%” on the webpage and “38%” on the PDF.

[10:18:30] Tyler Benson: Yep. Single source of truth.

[10:18:33] Simran Kaur: And make sure the diagram and copy agree on terms: “routing policy” vs “router.” People get weirdly literal.

[10:18:41] Markus Klein: I’ll review.

[10:18:43] Camila Reyes: Great. Let’s recap next steps.

[10:18:47] Camila Reyes: Ethan revises draft by Saturday EOD, focusing on leading with Northwind problem/constraints, tightening Why Redwood, removing over-precise claims until approved.

[10:18:58] Camila Reyes: Markus and Simran validate implementation details and diagram labels by Monday.

[10:19:03] Camila Reyes: Tyler drafts distribution checklist and UTM plan, plus standard metrics disclaimer and where it lives.

[10:19:10] Camila Reyes: Michael confirms allowable consent/disclaimer language for quotes and metrics.

[10:19:16] Camila Reyes: Then we aim to send to Northwind for review Tuesday.

[10:19:21] Soojin Lee: I’ll also rewrite the talk track snippet and subject line suggestions for outbound.

[10:19:27] Camila Reyes: Great add. Okay, thanks all.

[10:19:31] (crosstalk) Tyler Benson: Wait, sorry, one more—what’s the blog title?

[10:19:34] Soojin Lee: Placeholder: “How Northwind stabilized p95 latency on Dedicated inference (without blowing up cost).” Something like that.

[10:19:43] Camila Reyes: That’s good. Don’t over-promise. Alright, ending here.

---
End of transcript
